function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you put together the files you need, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, run `git` commands, or push commits from this environment.  
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can run locally, plus the exact file contents that you’ll want to add to the repo.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# From your terminal (make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub)
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you prefer HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a standard Node.js app (e.g. an `app.js` that listens on `process.env.PORT || 3000`), here’s a minimal Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json + lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Build the app (if you have a build step, otherwise skip)
# RUN npm run build

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` installs exactly what’s in `package-lock.json`, ensuring reproducible builds.  
> * The `EXPOSE 3000` line matches the typical Express default port.  
> * `CMD ["npm", "start"]` runs whatever script is defined under `"start"` in `package.json`.

> **If your app uses a different start script or port, adjust the `EXPOSE` and `CMD` lines accordingly.**

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change to your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to ClusterIP / NodePort if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your container.  
> * Exposes port 3000 inside the pod and maps it to port 80 on the service.  
> * Uses a `LoadBalancer` service type so you get an external IP (works on cloud providers).  
> * Adjust the `image:` field to point at the Docker image you’ll build/push.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image from the repo root (`context: .`).  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:latest`).  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret for authentication (no extra secrets needed).

> **If you want to push to Docker Hub instead**, replace the login and tags section with:

```yaml
    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: <your-dockerhub-username>/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

and make sure you store `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` as repo secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you created the `k8s` folder, you may need to `mkdir k8s` first.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to the registry you configured.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile added |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` added |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` added |
| ✅ | Files committed and pushed |

Feel free to tweak the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, or workflow to match any specific requirements your project has (different ports, environment variables, build steps, etc.). Once you push, you should see the workflow run in the “Actions” tab of your GitHub repo. Happy deploying!
